items.q: Explain the Android security model. How does the OS keep one app from touching another app's data?
shortAnswer: Each app runs as its own Linux UID in its own process, so app A literally cannot open app B's private files.
SELinux adds a second layer of control: even if file permissions allow an action, the kernel refuses it unless the process's policy domain permits it.
Sharing across apps only happens through permission-gated, user-approved channels — runtime permissions, content URIs, and explicit intents — never by default.
items.answer:
#### The sandbox
Every Android app runs as a unique Linux user ID (UID) inside its own process. The kernel's normal user/group model is the first wall: a UID's files, sockets, and shared memory are owned by that UID, so one app literally cannot open another's private data — an attempt gets `Permission denied` at the syscall level, before any Java code runs. IPC is confined to Binder, and intents are only delivered to components the manifest exposes. A buggy or malicious app is therefore contained: it can only touch what its own UID owns.

#### SELinux on top
SELinux is a second, independent layer of mandatory access control. Every process is assigned a security label, and the kernel enforces a policy of allowed actions per label — a *domain* — regardless of the classic Unix permission bits. Even where DAC would permit an operation, SELinux refuses it if the policy does not authorize it. Apps run in the `untrusted_app` domain; platform services get tightly scoped domains of their own, so a compromise in one service does not cascade into the others.

#### Where the model stops
It does not protect an app from its own bugs, does not survive a rooted device (root is the kernel's god-mode), and does not replace permissions. Sharing happens only through the sanctioned channels: `dangerous` runtime permissions the user grants, content URIs with per-access grants, and explicit intents to exported components. The one-line summary interviewers want: isolation by UID, containment by SELinux, sharing only through user-approved, permission-gated interfaces.

code.caption: Why app B's files are unreachable even from your own process

followUps: What can an app with the same signing certificate still not do to another of your apps without SELinux policy?
How does the sandbox protect your exported component from a malicious intent?
Where does the sandbox end — what survives a backup restore or an adb pull?
traps: Claiming the sandbox can be 'turned off' for performance — isolation by UID is not optional.
Saying SELinux is 'just file permissions' — it is a separate mandatory-access-control layer enforced by the kernel.

items.q: How does the Android Keystore keep a key non-exportable? What does StrongBox add? How does key attestation prove the key is real?
shortAnswer: `KeyGenerator` + `AndroidKeyStore` creates the key inside trusted hardware (TEE, or a secure element with `setIsStrongBoxBacked(true)`), and the key never leaves it.
`setUserAuthenticationRequired(true)` ties key use to biometric or device-credential unlock; you can allow a time window with `setUserAuthenticationValidityDurationSeconds`.
Key attestation proves the key is real hardware: a certificate chain rooted at Google (TEE) or StrongBox, signed at creation and bound to boot state.
items.answer:
#### Where the key lives
The `AndroidKeyStore` provider generates keys inside a **TEE** — a CPU-isolated trusted execution environment — and hands your process a handle, not key bytes. The key is created in hardware, used in hardware, and the raw material is never readable by your app. A rooted device, a memory dump, or an APK pull yields only the ability to *ask* the hardware to use the key, never the key itself. That is what 'non-exportable' means.

#### StrongBox
`setIsStrongBoxBacked(true)` in `KeyGenParameterSpec` moves the key into a dedicated secure element — the same class of hardware as a smart-card chip — rather than the general TEE. It is slower and has a finite key-use counter, but it is more isolated: a compromise of the TEE does not compromise it. Use it for high-value keys like payments; not every device has one, so keep a fallback.

#### setUserAuthenticationRequired
The Keystore can gate key use behind authentication: `setUserAuthenticationRequired(true)` plus `setInvalidatedByBiometricEnrollment(true)` (a newly enrolled fingerprint invalidates the key) and `setUserAuthenticationValidityDurationSeconds(...)` for a time window instead of per-use auth. The *hardware* enforces the gate — your code cannot bypass it.

#### Key attestation
Key attestation (`KeyStore.getCertificateChain` bound to a server-supplied challenge) returns an X.509 chain rooted at Google's key (TEE) or the vendor's StrongBox root, signed at generation time. A server verifies the chain and the attestation's boot-stated fields to prove the key was generated in genuine secure hardware on a verified-boot device — separating real key material from a software-keystore emulator.

code.caption: A StrongBox-backed, auth-gated key and its attestation chain
code.src:
private const val KEY_ALIAS = "pay_key"

fun createKey(): KeyGenParameterSpec =
    KeyGenParameterSpec.Builder(
        KEY_ALIAS,
        KeyProperties.PURPOSE_ENCRYPT or KeyProperties.PURPOSE_DECRYPT
    )
        .setBlockModes(KeyProperties.BLOCK_MODE_GCM)
        .setEncryptionPaddings(KeyProperties.ENCRYPTION_PADDING_NONE)
        .setUserAuthenticationRequired(true)
        .setInvalidatedByBiometricEnrollment(true)
        .setUserAuthenticationValidityDurationSeconds(30)
        .setIsStrongBoxBacked(true)
        .build()

fun attestationChain(): List<java.security.cert.Certificate> {
    val ks = KeyStore.getInstance("AndroidKeyStore").apply { load(null) }
    return ks.getCertificateChain(KEY_ALIAS).toList()
}

followUps: Why does key attestation need a fresh server challenge, and what does the attestation's boot-state field prove?
What happens to an auth-gated key when the user enrolls a new fingerprint?
When is the TEE not enough, and you want a server-side HSM instead?
traps: Saying the Keystore 'encrypts your data'. It holds keys; you still perform the encryption with a `Cipher`.
Claiming `setUserAuthenticationRequired(true)` alone blocks all offline attacks — the lock screen and the threat model still matter.

items.q: Jetpack Security's security-crypto is deprecated. How do you encrypt data at rest today? What do you gain?
shortAnswer: `security-crypto` (EncryptedSharedPreferences, EncryptedFile) was a Keystore convenience wrapper. It's deprecated now, so build on the raw Keystore APIs or a maintained library.
The pattern: a non-exportable Keystore AES/GCM key, a `Cipher` with a fresh random 12-byte IV, and store IV plus ciphertext, never hardcoded passphrase.
For a whole Room database, use SQLCipher as the SQLite driver with a Keystore-derived passphrase, and exclude secrets from auto-backup.
items.answer:
#### Why security-crypto is gone
Jetpack Security's `security-crypto` library wrapped the Keystore so encrypted preferences and files were a one-liner. Google deprecated it — the APIs are unmaintained — and the replacement is the underlying pattern it used. In an interview, citing it as *the* answer is a date check; the current answer is the raw-Keystore pattern below.

#### The pattern to describe
1. Generate an AES/GCM key in the `AndroidKeyStore` — non-exportable, optionally StrongBox-backed.
2. `Cipher.getInstance("AES/GCM/NoPadding")`, `init(ENCRYPT_MODE, key)`, read `cipher.iv`, and store **IV + ciphertext**. A fresh random IV per encryption is mandatory — a reused IV with GCM is a catastrophic, fully-recoverable break.
3. Never store the key and never derive it from a hardcoded passphrase — a hardcoded secret is recoverable from the APK, which is equivalent to no encryption.
4. For a whole database, SQLCipher encrypts every page; `Room.databaseBuilder(...).openHelperFactory(SQLCipherOpenHelperFactory(...))` swaps in with the same DAOs and migrations.

#### What you actually gain
At-rest encryption defends the stolen-device and forensics case: a `dd` of internal storage yields ciphertext, and the key lives only in the TEE. It does **not** defend an attacker running inside your app (same UID reads your plaintext after you decrypt), malware with root, or your own logs. So scope it — encrypt tokens, keys, and sensitive blobs; exclude them from backups; and keep the threat model honest: the client is still untrusted.

code.caption: Keystore AES/GCM encrypt/decrypt — IV travels with the ciphertext

followUps: Why is reusing an IV with AES/GCM a fatal flaw, not a subtle one?
What does SQLCipher give you that encrypting individual values doesn't?
How do you keep a token out of Google Drive auto-backup without breaking device migration?
traps: Recommending security-crypto as the current solution — it is deprecated.
Answering 'we use AES' without a key-management story; where the key lives is the whole question.

items.q: How do you build biometric login with BiometricPrompt? When do you attach a CryptoObject? Why does Class 3 matter?
shortAnswer: Check capability first: `BiometricManager.canAuthenticate(BIOMETRIC_STRONG or DEVICE_CREDENTIAL)` must return success before you show the system prompt; deep-link enrollment when nothing is enrolled.
A `CryptoObject` wraps a `Cipher` over `setUserAuthenticationRequired(true)` key; the TEE releases the key only after genuine authentication, binding the result to your operation.
Class 3 (`BIOMETRIC_STRONG`) means strong biometrics; weaker Class 2 cannot use crypto-bound keys, so the choice trades UX against assurance.
items.answer:
#### The flow
Check availability before showing anything: `BiometricManager.from(context).canAuthenticate(BIOMETRIC_STRONG or DEVICE_CREDENTIAL)` — `BIOMETRIC_SUCCESS` means you may prompt; `BIOMETRIC_ERROR_NONE_ENROLLED` means the user has no credential set up and you deep-link enrollment. Then build `PromptInfo` with `setAllowedAuthenticators(...)`. Including `DEVICE_CREDENTIAL` is what lets the PIN/pattern/password fallback happen *inside the same system prompt* — the honest path for a user with no biometric.

#### Why CryptoObject
A bare prompt proves only that a biometric gesture happened; nothing ties it to your data. A `CryptoObject` wraps a `Cipher`, `Mac`, or `Signature` over a Keystore key created with `setUserAuthenticationRequired(true)`. The hardware releases the key for `Cipher.init(DECRYPT_MODE, ...)` only after a genuine successful authentication — so you can decrypt a stored token in the success callback and know the auth was real, not replayed. No `CryptoObject`, no cryptographic binding.

#### Class 2 vs Class 3
Class 3 is strong: fingerprint, secure 3D face, iris. Class 2 is weaker face/voice that is cheaper to spoof. Strong-biometric-protected keys require Class 3 — passing `BIOMETRIC_STRONG` declares it. If you allow Class 2 (`BIOMETRIC_WEAK`), crypto-bound authentication is off the table entirely. Combine the class choice with `CryptoObject` and `setUserAuthenticationValidityDurationSeconds` for re-auth windows, and keep a real fallback — re-entry of a server-side password — for the failure path.

code.caption: BiometricPrompt with a crypto-bound decrypt

followUps: Why is a crypto-bound key invalidated when the user adds a new biometric?
How do you keep the prompt alive across a configuration change like rotation?
What is the difference between DEVICE_CREDENTIAL in setAllowedAuthenticators and the old setDeviceCredentialAllowed?
traps: Treating the prompt result as proof of identity for arbitrary data — without a CryptoObject the auth isn't bound to any key or operation.
Allowing Class 2 biometrics for a strong-protected key — the platform rejects the crypto operation at runtime.

items.q: Play Integrity replaced SafetyNet. What signal does it give you? What does it prove? Where should the verdict be checked?
shortAnswer: Play Integrity returns a Google-signed, nonce-bound verdict with three signals: app integrity (your signed APK from Play), device integrity (bootloader state), and licensing.
SafetyNet Attestation is deprecated; Play Integrity is its successor — more signals, and the JWS is verified with Google's keys or the Play Console API.
Verify on your backend, not client-side: the verdict is a device-state risk signal for fraud detection, never proof of who holds the device.
items.answer:
#### The three signals
Play Integrity returns a Google-signed JSON verdict with: **app integrity** — the running APK is the one you signed and Play distributed; **device integrity** — bootloader state and no root/compromise-indicating flags, with Play services running; and **licensing/account details**. The token is bound to a nonce you supply, short-lived, and signed by Google, so it cannot be forged or replayed.

#### Vs SafetyNet
SafetyNet Attestation is deprecated; Play Integrity is the successor. The practical differences: Play Integrity adds app-integrity and licensing signals SafetyNet lacked, and its verification story is standardized — verify the JWS signature with Google's public keys or call the Play Console API from your server. Migrating is mostly issuing a new token and verifying the new format.

#### What it does NOT prove
The list interviews reward you for stating: a passing verdict does not prove the *user* is legitimate (device farms attest real hardware), does not stop a determined attacker (device-and-response replay, Frida attached after the call, a modified build on a device the check flags later), and is not 'this person is trustworthy'. It is a point-in-time statement that *this app instance is in a known-good state*. Use it as one signal in a server-side risk engine alongside anomaly detection.

#### Where to check
The verdict must be verified server-side: the client sends app + token, your server validates the signature and nonce, reads the verdict, and only then raises the user's trust level. Checking client-side is theater — a tampered client tampers with the check too.

code.caption: Client collects the token; the server is the only verifier

followUps: What is the difference between MEETS_DEVICE_INTEGRITY and MEETS_STRONG_INTEGRITY?
How do you handle a user whose verdict fails — block outright or degrade their trust level?
Why should the nonce be generated server-side and bound to the session?
traps: Trusting a verdict checked inside the app — the check must run somewhere the attacker doesn't control.
Presenting Play Integrity as identity or anti-fraud proof rather than a device-state signal.

items.q: You're asked to detect rooted devices client-side. How would you approach it? Why is that approach fragile?
shortAnswer: Every client-side check runs on the attacker's machine, where it can be hooked or spoofed — root detection is a losing arms race.
The realistic pattern: cheap, fragile signals — test-keys, su binaries, known packages — feed a risk score, alongside Play Integrity's device verdict verified server-side.
Treat root as a risk factor to weigh and degrade around, never something to block on — a blocking client just gets its check stripped.
items.answer:
#### Why it's fragile
Root detection runs on the attacker's machine. Any check you write — `ro.build.tags` containing `test-keys`, an `su` binary on PATH, the Magisk package, overlayfs traces, `/system/xbin` — can be read, hooked (Frida, LSPosed), spoofed, or bypassed by Zygisk deny-lists while the real app runs elsewhere. A rooted attacker controls the responses; a bypass is an afternoon of work. Treat any single check as noise, not proof.

#### What still earns a place
Use the checks as **cheap signals in a stack**, not a binary gate: test-keys property, known-bad package names, su binary locations, suspicious mounts, and your own APK signature at runtime. Fail closed where the cost is low — require re-authentication or block one high-value action — and log the score server-side with a version tag. Accept false positives: some legitimate users run admin tools, custom ROMs, or a corporate MDM that trips your heuristics.

#### The platform answer
The strongest signal available is Play Integrity's device-integrity verdict — bootloader state and Play services health — which is Google-signed and server-verifiable, and far harder to fake than a file check. But even it can be gamed with device farming, so it remains a risk indicator, not identity.

#### The realism the interview tests
The right framing: root detection is a **risk indicator feeding a server-side risk engine**, never a statement of truth, never enforced purely on the device. Anyone promising 'we detect root and block' client-side is describing a demo, not a defense.

code.caption: Cheap client signals that feed a server-side risk score — never a gate

followUps: Why is Play Integrity's device verdict more trustworthy than a file existence check?
How do you keep a rooted user usable while still protecting the highest-risk actions?
What is the cost of a false positive for a legitimate user?
traps: Promising root detection as a solvable problem — the environment is attacker-controlled.
Blocking users purely on a client-side check, which the attacker simply removes.

items.q: Two exported components forward the intents they receive to internal Activities. What is intent redirection? How do you audit for it?
shortAnswer: Intent redirection: an exported component re-launches a received intent or hands it to a `PendingIntent`, carrying the attacker's target, URI, and grant flags.
The payoff is a URI permission grant, or a privileged action run as your UID: the attacker borrows your authority without ever asking you.
Audit: never forward a received `Intent`; copy validated fields into a fresh one, clear flags, drop `FLAG_GRANT_*_URI_PERMISSION`, enable StrictMode's `detectUnsafeIntentLaunch` in debug.
items.answer:
#### The chain
An exported component is reachable by any app — that is its definition. The vulnerable pattern is forwarding: `startActivity(intent)` on the very Intent you received. That Intent still carries the attacker's component target, action, extras, and — the real payload — URI permission grant flags such as `FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION`. The system honours those grants because *your* UID is performing the launch, so an attacker who gets your component to forward a crafted intent can read a content URI your app never meant to share, or steer an internal component into an action it shouldn't take. The same chain works through `PendingIntent` and `getActivity` — anywhere a received Intent is re-invoked.

#### What the platform changed
Since Android 14, apps targeting 34+ cannot send an **implicit** intent that resolves to one of their own non-exported components — that specific self-navigation hole is closed by the system. An explicit forward, or a forward into a system component, is still on you. The change reduces blast radius; it does not remove the bug class.

#### The audit checklist
- `exported="false"` unless you can name the caller and the use case.
- In any exported component, never re-launch the received Intent — copy the fields you validated into a fresh one.
- Strip flags (`intent.flags = 0` unless you re-add them deliberately) and drop the two grant flags.
- `StrictMode.setVmPolicy(VmPolicy.Builder().detectUnsafeIntentLaunch())` catches forwards at dev time.
- Check `getCallingPackage()` against an allowlist inside the component.

code.caption: Exported component that validates input and never forwards the Intent

followUps: How does a URI permission grant survive the forward — why is that the attack's payload?
What did Android 14's implicit-intent block actually fix, and what did it leave open?
How would you find an intent-redirection bug in a legacy codebase?
traps: Forwarding the received Intent unchanged and assuming the framework re-validates — grants and flags travel with it.
Treating exported=false as the whole fix — the explicit forward and the PendingIntent variants remain.

items.q: Why is every PendingIntent you hand out immutable by default? What does FLAG_MUTABLE let the recipient do?
shortAnswer: A `PendingIntent` is a capability token: whoever holds it can fire your Intent as your app. Since Android 12 it's immutable by default.
`FLAG_MUTABLE` lets the holder change the Intent's action, data, component, and extras before it fires — a redirection primitive in a malicious holder's hands.
`FLAG_MUTABLE` is needed where the system must fill a field itself — notification direct reply, some widget and assistant flows — use it only there.
items.answer:
#### The token model
A `PendingIntent` wraps an Intent and a component, and grants whoever holds the token the right to fire it **as your app**: `getCreatorPackage()` returns your package, the launch runs with your UID, and URI grants on it are honoured with your authority. It is a capability, so the default posture since Android 12 is `FLAG_IMMUTABLE` — the holder cannot touch the wrapped Intent's contents.

#### What mutability buys an attacker
With `FLAG_MUTABLE`, the holder can `fillIn`/`send` a modified Intent: change the component target, inject extras, or attach a data URI carrying a grant flag. A mutable PendingIntent handed to a system API that passes it onward, or exposed through an exported surface, becomes an intent-redirection primitive — an attacker steers *your* token at a component you never meant to reach, running as you. That is why the platform made the flag mandatory to declare when targeting Android 12+ and immutable the default: the dangerous value now has to be explicit.

#### When mutable is genuinely required
The short list: notification **direct reply** (`RemoteInput` must inject the reply text), some `AppWidgetProvider` click flows the system augments, and certain `getActivity`-for-result patterns. The rule: immutable everywhere, mutable exactly where the API breaks without it, no URI grants on a mutable token, and a code review for every mutable creation. The default incantation should read `FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT or FLAG_IMMUTABLE`.

code.caption: Immutable by default; mutable only for RemoteInput
code.src:
val contentIntent = Intent(context, InboxActivity::class.java)
val defaultPi = PendingIntent.getActivity(
    context, 0, contentIntent,
    PendingIntent.FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT or PendingIntent.FLAG_IMMUTABLE
)

// The one legitimate mutable case: RemoteInput must write the reply into the Intent.
val replyIntent = Intent(context, ReplyReceiver::class.java)
val replyPi = PendingIntent.getBroadcast(
    context, 1, replyIntent,
    PendingIntent.FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT or PendingIntent.FLAG_MUTABLE
)
val action = NotificationCompat.Action.Builder(
    R.drawable.ic_reply, "Reply", replyPi
).addRemoteInput(RemoteInput.Builder(KEY_REPLY).build()).build()

followUps: Beyond notifications, what can a malicious holder do with a mutable PendingIntent?
How do URI grants interact with a mutable PendingIntent?
Which Android version forced the explicit mutability flag, and what does targeting lower change?
traps: Marking a PendingIntent mutable 'in case we need it later' — every mutable token is a redirection surface.
Claiming FLAG_IMMUTABLE prevents the creator from reusing the token — it only binds the recipient.

items.q: Custom schemes and unverified https links both get hijacked. What makes a link hijack-resistant? What does assetlinks.json verify?
shortAnswer: A custom scheme is a first-come claim: any app can declare the same filter, so a chooser appears and hijacking is trivial by design.
An Android App Link is https with `android:autoVerify=true`, checked at install against `https://<host>/.well-known/assetlinks.json` — listing package name, SHA-256 signing-certificate fingerprint.
Wrong fingerprint (Play App Signing vs upload key), a redirect, or wrong content type silently fails verification, degrading the link so other apps can intercept.
items.answer:
#### Why schemes are hijackable
An intent filter is a claim, not a right. For a custom scheme, every app can register `myapp://`, and because several apps match, Android shows a disambiguation dialog. An attacker registers your scheme, captures the user's 'always open with', or redirects a link rendered in a WebView. There is no ownership model for schemes — treating one as identity is the bug.

#### App Links raise the bar
An App Link is an `https://your-domain/...` filter with `android:autoVerify="true"`. At install time (and periodically) Android fetches `https://your-domain/.well-known/assetlinks.json` and checks that it declares your package name and a SHA-256 of your **signing certificate**. On a match the system opens your app directly — no chooser — and a competing app cannot claim that link. Ownership moves from 'whoever installed first' to 'whoever controls the domain', which is the entire point.

#### The failure modes
Verification failing is silent and the link degrades to *unverified* — the chooser returns and other apps can intercept. Common causes: the file isn't served as `application/json` from the exact path, the request redirects, the fingerprint uses your upload key instead of the Play App Signing key, or an HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect on the host. Debug with `adb shell pm verify-app-links` and `get-app-links`.

#### Verification is not safety
Even a verified App Link is an attacker-controllable entry point — a shared link can carry hostile parameters. assetlinks.json proves ownership of the mapping, nothing about the payload; every parameter is still untrusted input.

code.caption: Verified App Link filter, and treating the payload as hostile
code.src:
<!-- AndroidManifest.xml -->
<activity android:name=".ItemActivity" android:exported="true" android:launchMode="singleTop">
    <intent-filter android:autoVerify="true">
        <action android:name="android.intent.action.VIEW" />
        <category android:name="android.intent.category.DEFAULT" />
        <category android:name="android.intent.category.BROWSABLE" />
        <data android:scheme="https" android:host="example.com" android:pathPrefix="/item" />
    </intent-filter>
</activity>

// Even a verified link is hostile input — validate every field.
fun handleAppLink(intent: Intent) {
    val itemId = intent.data?.lastPathSegment
        ?.takeIf { it.matches(Regex("[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,32}")) } ?: return
    openItem(itemId)
}

followUps: Why does the Play App Signing fingerprint mismatch make App Link verification silently fail?
What happens when verification can't complete at install, and how do you detect it?
What is still left to secure once you accept that a link is user-controllable input?
traps: Claiming assetlinks.json proves 'the link is safe' — it proves ownership, not that the payload is benign.
Using a custom scheme for anything sensitive because 'nobody else would register it'.

items.q: You're loading untrusted remote content into a WebView. What is the full hardening list? What do you lose by applying it?
shortAnswer: Untrusted content: JavaScript off unless needed, `setAllowFileAccess(false)`, `setAllowContentAccess(false)`, no file URLs, `WebViewAssetLoader` to serve assets over https, no `file://`.
Never `addJavascriptInterface` on untrusted pages — it's the classic RCE channel. If you must bridge, keep it to trusted first-party pages with the smallest surface.
Add Safe Browsing for known-malicious pages, verify the origin before any privileged action, and treat the WebView as hostile — no credentials or native secrets.
items.answer:
#### The baseline
For untrusted remote content: `settings.javaScriptEnabled = false` unless a feature genuinely needs it; `setAllowFileAccess(false)`, `setAllowContentAccess(false)`, `setAllowFileAccessFromFileURLs(false)`, `setAllowUniversalAccessFromFileURLs(false)`; and turn off geolocation, zoom, and other surfaces you don't need. Everything the page can read is data you handed it, so hand it nothing you wouldn't paste into a browser.

#### JavaScript interfaces
`addJavascriptInterface` injects Java methods as `window.<name>` — the single most dangerous WebView API. Before Android 4.2 it was remotely exploitable (the classic WebView RCE); since then only `@JavascriptInterface`-annotated methods are exposed, but the risk moves to what those methods can do. A page that can reach your bridge can call anything annotated. So: never bridge untrusted pages, and when a first-party page genuinely needs it, expose one method with no `Context`, no file paths, and validated arguments. Prefer `postMessage`/`WebMessageListener` or `evaluateJavascript` for the rare data you actually need.

#### Files, schemes, Safe Browsing
A WebView that renders remote HTML must not be able to read `file://` or `content://` — that turns the browser into a local-file reader. Keep both off and serve your own bundled assets through `WebViewAssetLoader`, which presents them over an https scheme (`appassets.androidplatform.net`) the page can load without file access. Enable Safe Browsing (`SafeBrowsingCompat`) so Google's lists block known-malicious pages. Finally, verify `webView.url` matches your host before any privileged action in `onPageFinished` — navigation is the other way in: a redirect chain to an attacker host is still 'your WebView'.

code.caption: Hardened untrusted-content WebView with an https asset loader

followUps: Why is addJavascriptInterface the one thing you must never do with untrusted content?
How does WebViewAssetLoader keep local assets reachable while file access stays off?
What can the WebView still leak even with all of this locked down?
traps: Enabling JavaScript plus a bridge 'for convenience' on remote content — that is the RCE class.
Thinking file access being off makes your assets unreachable — route them through the https loader instead of re-opening file://.
